article.title: Content modelling for headless: getting it wrong, then right
article.excerpt: The single biggest determinant of whether a headless rollout ships on time. A field guide to dynamic zones, components, and the conversations to have with editors before you touch the schema.

article.title: Draft & Publish in production — what the docs don't tell you
article.excerpt: Editor workflows, preview URLs, and the surprisingly subtle interplay with Next.js draft mode. Notes from running this at scale across two enterprise rollouts.

article.title: Migrating from Contentful to Strapi without a freeze
article.excerpt: How we moved 40 editorial brands off Contentful and onto Strapi 5 with zero content freeze, zero URL changes, and (mostly) zero tears. Includes the migration script we open-sourced.

article.title: Why your Next.js ISR is lying to you (and how to fix it)
article.excerpt: A short investigation into stale-while-revalidate behaviour in App Router and the three configuration mistakes I see most often.

article.title: Building High-Performance Strapi Apps: Common Pitfalls and Best Practices
article.excerpt: Where Strapi performance problems actually come from, why populate=deep is a trap, and how to design schemas that don't get expensive as they grow.

article.title: Strapi 5 + Next.js App Router — the integration patterns that actually scale
article.excerpt: Six patterns I keep reaching for when wiring Strapi 5 to a real Next.js App Router codebase. Tagged revalidation, draft mode handoff, the typed client, and what to do about RSC.
article.intro: Most enterprise headless rollouts don't fail at the technical level. They fail in the gap between the content model the engineering team designs in week two and the editorial workflows that emerge in production six months later. This piece is about closing that gap — specifically, the integration patterns I've seen survive contact with reality on Strapi 5 and Next.js App Router.

blocks.heading: The typed client
blocks.body: Generate types from your Strapi schema and check them in. The cost is one CI step; the benefit is that every breaking content-model change shows up as a TypeScript error in the Next.js codebase before it ever reaches preview. Don't write the client by hand — use the OpenAPI export.

blocks.text: If your editors don't trust the preview, they will work around the CMS. The architecture battle is lost in the editor's chair, not the IDE.

blocks.heading: Tagged revalidation
blocks.body: Forget time-based ISR. Tag every fetch with the content type and entry slug, and let the Strapi lifecycle hooks call revalidateTag on publish. Pages stay static, edits feel instant, your CDN bill stays small. Two lines per content type.

blocks.title: src/api/article/content-types/article/lifecycles.ts

blocks.heading: Draft mode, properly
blocks.body: Draft mode in App Router needs three things to work end-to-end with Strapi: a signed token from the CMS, a server route that sets the cookie, and a layout that reads it to switch the API call. I'll show you the smallest correct implementation.

faq.question: Are you a contractor or a Strapi employee?
faq.answer: I'm employed full-time as Implementation Manager at Strapi. This site is my own: anything I take on independently is separate from that role and cleared with my employer, and the work and case studies here are mine, not Strapi's. If what you need is Strapi's own support or services, that's a conversation to have with Strapi directly rather than with me.

faq.question: Do you only work on Strapi projects?
faq.answer: Mostly. I'll occasionally take an interim tech lead role on a wider JS-ecosystem project, but only if there's a clear headless-content angle. I won't be the right fit for, say, a Rails monolith or a mobile-only product.

faq.question: Where are you based, and do you travel?
faq.answer: UK-based, fully remote. I travel for kick-offs, key workshops, and post-mortems where it helps; most enterprise clients see me on-site for the moments that matter during delivery.

faq.question: What about smaller teams or pre-seed startups?
faq.answer: Sometimes. My independent work is scoped for teams with a real platform need and their own engineers, so I'm not always the right fit for an early-stage team. The free 30-minute discovery call is open to anyone, and I'll tell you honestly if the open-source resources will get you where you need to go without me.

faq.question: Can you supply other engineers?
faq.answer: No. I'm one person and that's the point. When scope needs more hands I'll say so early and help you find them, but I won't quietly subcontract — you'll always know who's doing the work.

principle.title: The team owns it
principle.description: If your engineers can't operate the platform without me by the end of the engagement, I haven't done my job. The leverage is in transferring competence, not gating it.

principle.title: Boring infrastructure
principle.description: I will reach for the proven tool over the interesting one almost every time. Strapi, Postgres, Vercel. The boring stack survives staff turnover; the clever one rarely does.

principle.title: Editor-led modelling
principle.description: Content models that don't match how editors actually work get worked around. I spend disproportionate time with editorial teams in week one.

principle.title: Written, not whispered
principle.description: Every architectural decision lives in a written ADR. Every meeting outcome lives in a doc. The best documentation is the kind that survives me leaving.

process-phase.title: Discovery call
process-phase.description: 30-minute free call. We figure out if I'm the right fit. If not, I'll tell you who is.

process-phase.title: Listening
process-phase.description: Stakeholder interviews, content audit, infra read. I produce a written engagement brief before we touch a line of code.

process-phase.title: Architecture
process-phase.description: Content model, integration approach, plugin choices, deployment plan. Reviewed with your engineers, not over them.

process-phase.title: Delivery
process-phase.description: Embedded with your team. Weekly demos, two-week feedback cadence, your engineers in the driver's seat by week eight.

process-phase.title: Handover
process-phase.description: Runbooks, training sessions, on-call shadowing. I'm out the door once your team is faster without me. Quarterly reviews available.
